Phil, can you please talk about the data center that is moving forward with construction in saline Michigan despite its citizens voting against it. 

The residents of Saline Michigan voted against the data center being put in. The developers of the data center filed a multi-million dollar lawsuit against the city that it couldn’t afford to force construction to continue. 

The residents, upon finding out the city settled the lawsuit privately, tried to intervene as there was no vote taken to approve the settlement. Their intervention was denied for being past the 30 day mark. They didn’t know they needed to intervene until the deadline had already passed. 

The data center claimed irreparable harm because they had already paid a non-refundable $40 million deposit to DTE (electric company who just hiked up our rates again, btw) and had already ordered $2 billion in equipment. 

These people are plowing through our small towns who can’t afford to stop them. People are voting against it, and their votes are being silenced and tossed aside. This is the beginning of the fall of our democracy. Our votes hold less weight every single day. This should be taken very seriously.

comments.text:
As someone who’s studied a bit of business law which covers trademarks and copyrights. This whole saga has really been frustrating to me regarding people’s sweeping claims and assertions about the subject. Intellectual property (IP) protections are absolutely essential for creating an environment that encourages and protects ideas and “identity” for broadly speaking commercial interest. The “commercial interest” or I believe the wording in law is “in commerce” is the important bit. 

Brands have “identity,” and no, I don’t mean this in a weird legalistic “corporations are people” way but in a recognition way. If we play some word association and say: “I’m loving it,” “finger lickin’ good,” or “taste the rainbow,” many people would immediately guess McDonald’s, KFC, and Skittles respectively. Because those brands have made those jingles, slogans, even designs part of their identity. I can abstract it even more if I specify an industry and say: “jewelry and blue,” people think Tiffany.

Now this seems like it massively benefits only big corporations, but no, trademarks are crucial for small business and individuals. If my last name is McDonald and I create a small moving company: McDonald’s movers or smtn, McDonald’s can’t come and sue me for infringement. Not because I added another word, but because trademarks are tied to industries. Me being a moving company and McDonald being a food company, there’s no overlap, so no infringement. However, if I start “encroaching” on the McDonald’s brand; I adopt a similar arch logo, similar colours, use the jingle in an ad. Now this is encroachment, because I’m trying to “tie” or “associate” my company with McDonald’s established brand and identity. 

Now, I know I started the last paragraph saying it doesn’t disproportionately benefit large corporations… However, due to the sheer scale of some modern top companies and the reality that some people would create similarly named companies to “piggyback” or capitalize on the already famous brand’s reputation, massive companies do have “extra” protections within their respective industries. For starters, phonetically similar names and “misspelled” versions are covered under their trademark protections. This is because of a thing called “likelihood of confusion,” because someone just hearing the name or even quickly scanning a shelf might experience momentary confusion. The clothing and fashion industry are aggressive enforcers of this. Because there is already a long history and culture of knockoffs and dupes that try and intentionally get “close” to the design and spelling of an existing and established brand. 

All this to say, Pattie does not have a strong case against Patagonia. Immediately, we have to recognize it’s filed in the same class of goods. The name being somewhat phonetically similar compounds on that making it a high hurdle to try and argue against. As a side note for anyone claiming it has parody protection, that would be wrong. Parody protects non commercial endeavours and filing a trademark to sell clothing and merchandise certainly indicates a commercial intent. I believe Patagonia also shared (“cherry picked” according to Pattie) screenshots of people already asking if there is official partnership or collaborations, which only builds onto a proof of confusion between the brands for consumers. The “informal agreement” wouldn’t even be an important factor given everything else. Then finally, this isn’t likely to play into anything legal, I just find it sketchy. Pattie apparently filed this all the way back in January, Patagonia has been trying to handle it quietly since then. Pattie brought this to light only very recently… near the start of pride month. It just feels a bit shady trying to weaponize the narrative that “big corporation is trying to destroy a queer creator trying to build a small business.” 

Now this last bit is just a comment. I agree with someone people that current IP protection laws and rules should be changed and updated, however I fundamentally disagree with someone people who argue that this is showing the system being abused. It’s not. I guarantee if there was a prominent minority owned company that got their branding co-opted in a way by an alt right group, people would be outraged and argue for more protections.
